name: らーめん 遊貯 (Ramen Yucho)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the soy-sauce tare is normally wheat-based, so the dish is not gluten-free and no GF accommodation is indicated.
The bowl is a ginger soy-sauce ramen built on a special ginger shoyu tare, which in Japanese ramen is virtually always brewed from wheat-containing soy sauce.
The broth is a fish/dashi base (horse mackerel, mackerel, bonito) and toppings include pork chashu and roast beef, so cross-contact with animal products is inherent to every bowl.
Built entirely around house-made wheat ramen noodles; flour is handled and cooked on-site, so cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable.
Jiro-style tare is soy-sauce based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Articles describe a soy/salt-balanced broth.
Pork broth and pork toppings are central to the bowls; no vegan or vegetarian preparation found.

name: らーめんや たみん (Ramenya Tamin)

claims.text: Single small counter run by one person serving wheat-noodle ramen; no separate preparation area, so gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.
All bowls are built on animal broth (chicken / chicken-pork bone) with pork chashu; no plant-based options, and everything shares the same pots.
House specialty is wheat-noodle tantan-men prepared in a shared Sichuan/Chinese kitchen alongside other wheat-containing dishes (yakisoba, etc.); no gluten-free handling was documented.
Sichuan and Chinese cooking here relies on standard wheat-based soy sauce and fermented bean paste; no wheat-free seasoning alternatives were mentioned.
Tantan-men contains pork mince and the menu centers on meat and animal stocks; no vegan/vegetarian preparation or separation was noted.
Karashi soba is wheat-noodle based with a wheat mustard/soy ankake; gyoza and spring rolls are wheat-wrapped, and a small shared kitchen means no gluten isolation is possible.
The signature dish uses a soy-based ankake sauce (Japanese soy sauce contains wheat).
Broth is chicken-bone and kombu based, with chicken and shrimp in the dish; no vegan preparation exists, so all cookware contacts animal products.
Sichuan Chinese cooking of this style relies on wheat-based soy sauce and seasonings; no gluten-free soy alternative is indicated.
Vegetable dishes are cooked in shared woks alongside pork, chicken and seafood and commonly use meat-based stock and animal-derived seasonings; no vegan-separation practice is indicated.
Signature and most dishes use wheat noodles and wheat-based Chinese sauces; shared woks and a shared fryer mean pervasive gluten cross-contact. No gluten-free handling is documented.
Standard Chinese cooking here relies on soy sauce and bean/oyster-style sauces, which are wheat-containing; no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated.

The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward (the signature bowl centers on fried chicken and chicken oil); vegetable dishes are cooked in shared woks likely with animal-based stock/sauces, so no reliable vegan preparation can be confirmed.

name: 更科 聖護院支店 (Sarashina Shogoin-shiten)

claims.text: A wheat-noodle and soba/udon kitchen with shared boiling water and prep; no gluten-free handling indicated, so cross-contact should be assumed.
The light, Japanese-leaning broth and donburi seasonings almost certainly use standard wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free tare or seasoning is mentioned.
Broth and toppings are built on pork chashu and fish cake; even the noodle bowls are not vegetarian, and no separate vegan prep exists.
